A.explanation: Work by $F$ is $F \times d = 25 \times 0.50 = 12.5 \text{ J} \approx 13 \text{ J}$ because force and displacement are in the same forward direction.

B.explanation: This divides force by distance, $25 / 0.50 = 50$, instead of multiplying force by distance for work done.

C.explanation: This is the weight $mg \approx 70 \times 9.81$ times $0.50 \text{ m}$, but weight acts vertically and does no work on the forward motion.

D.explanation: This adds the $70 \text{ kg}$ weight to the $25 \text{ N}$ push before multiplying by $0.50 \text{ m}$, but only $F = 25 \text{ N}$ does the forward work asked for.

hints: Notice the arrow $F = 25 \text{ N}$ points forwards and the $0.50 \text{ m}$ travel is also forwards, so the force and displacement are parallel.
Recall work done by a constant force is $W = Fd\cos\theta$, and the $70 \text{ kg}$ total mass is not needed to find the work done by $F$ itself.
Multiply $25 \text{ N}$ by $0.50 \text{ m}$ to get joules, and check you have not divided or replaced $F$ with $mg$.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: work done by the forward force $F$, not by weight. Useful data are $F = 25 \text{ N}$ in the forward direction and forward displacement $d = 0.50 \text{ m}$ while the foot pushes.
State the rule: for a constant force parallel to displacement, $W = Fd\cos\theta$ with $\theta = 0$, so $W = Fd$. The $70 \text{ kg}$ mass would give weight, which is perpendicular to motion.
Substitute with units: $W = 25 \text{ N} \times 0.50 \text{ m} = 12.5 \text{ N m}$.
Convert and round: $1 \text{ N m} = 1 \text{ J}$, so $12.5 \text{ J}$ to two significant figures is about $13 \text{ J}$.
Connect to options: $13 \text{ J}$ matches the $F \times d$ result, while $50 \text{ J}$ comes from dividing and $340 \text{ J}$ and $360 \text{ J}$ come from bringing in weight. This is option A.
